node.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
node.description: Reconstructs women’s work before and during industrialization through household production, wages, training and agricultural change. She emphasizes unequal disruption while arguing for eventual benefits, a position distinct from Clark’s account of capitalist development.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930; new preface in the 1969 reprint). The original preface acknowledges Eileen Power’s direction of the research and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance.
node.scope_note: The complete 1930 introduction distinguishes paid visibility from productive work itself and separates married women, single women and workers supporting families. Power directs the acknowledged research; Knowles gives early guidance and Dorothy George supplies specific evidence. The 1969 preface, signed 1968, calls for later occupational research without supplying it. The broad optimistic conclusion remains an attributed argument; most occupational chapters and the original conclusion are unread.

sources.title: Alice Clark, Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion.
sources.citation: Alice Clark, Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion.

verification.note: Complete preface, introduction pp. 1–13 and conclusion pp. 290–308 read. Credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished material; distinguishes overlapping production forms, class and marital position, and paid/unpaid work. Acknowledges conjectural medieval comparisons and tentative causal conclusions. Maternal, racial and civilizational assumptions are historical commitments, not adopted facts. Main occupational chapters unread; quoted Pepys material in conclusion is mediated by Clark.

verification.note: Copyright and introduction pp. vii–xxii read, not the whole introduction or its bibliography. sources.title: Ivy Pinchbeck: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution
sources.citation: Ivy Pinchbeck, Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (George Routledge & Sons, 1930; reprint with new preface, Frank Cass, 1969).

verification.note: Additional publisher-preview reading: complete original preface vi, complete introduction pp. 1–5, 1969 reprint preface signed October 1968, and opening chapter I p. 7. Distinguishes occupational visibility, family wages, training, marital status, disruption and claimed eventual gains. Names Knowles, Power, scholarship support and George. The later preface proposes post-1850 research rather than supplying it. Remaining occupational chapters and conclusion unread; optimistic generalization is attributed, not independently proven. Previous scope: Publisher-distributed preview: copyright page confirms 1930 original and 1969 reprint; original preface p. vi acknowledges Eileen Power’s research direction and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance; introduction pp. 1–2 addresses women’s work before industrialization. Full book and later reception not audited.
